Biblical Meditation
BIB-lih-kuhl med-ih-TAY-shun
n.
“Meditation” from Latin meditari, “to think over, ponder, rehearse”; rendering the Hebrew hāgāh (to murmur, muse, ponder) and síach (to muse, talk to oneself).

Biblical Definition

Biblical meditation is the believer’s deliberate, prayerful pondering of God—His Word, His works, His character, and His ways—turning them over in the mind and pressing them upon the heart until they warm the affections and shape the life. It is utterly distinct from, and indeed the opposite of, the Eastern and mystical ‘meditation’ that seeks to empty the mind; biblical meditation fills the mind with the truth of God. The Hebrew words picture it vividly: hāgāh means to murmur or mutter, as one repeating words half-aloud to himself, chewing on them; síach means to muse and converse with oneself. The blessed man of the first psalm is one whose delight is in the law of the LORD, and who in His law doth meditate day and night—like a tree planted by rivers of water, drawing constant nourishment. The hundred-nineteenth psalm overflows with it: ‘O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day’; ‘I will meditate in thy precepts’; ‘mine eyes prevent the night watches, that I might meditate in thy word.’ The object of meditation is chiefly God’s Word, but also His works of creation and providence (‘I meditate on all thy works’) and His person and perfections. Its method is to read or recall a portion of truth, to ponder it deeply, to apply it to one’s own heart and circumstances, and to turn it into prayer and praise. Its purpose is transformation: meditation is the bridge between reading and praying, between the truth in the head and the truth in the heart; it is the digestion of spiritual food, by which the Word read or heard is assimilated into the soul and made to nourish faith, love, and obedience. The Puritans accounted meditation among the most important and most neglected of the disciplines, the means by which truth descends from the understanding into the affections and the will. To meditate on God’s Word day and night is the mark of the blessed man and the secret of a fruitful, stable, God-centered life.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MEDITATION as close or continued thought; the turning or revolving of a subject in the mind; serious contemplation, especially on religious or sacred subjects.

expand to see more

MEDITATION, n. — 1. Close or continued thought; the turning or revolving of a subject in the mind; serious contemplation. 2. Contemplation of spiritual or sacred things... It is sometimes employed devotionally, in fixing the mind on the divine character, works and will.

MEDITATE, v.i. — To dwell on any thing in thought; to contemplate; to study; to turn or revolve any subject in the mind.

Key Scripture

Psalm 1:2 — "But his delight is in the law of the Lord; and in his law doth he meditate day and night."

Joshua 1:8 — "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein."

Psalm 119:97 — "O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day."

Psalm 143:5 — "I remember the days of old; I meditate on all thy works; I muse on the work of thy hands."

Modern Corruption

Biblical meditation is corrupted by the Eastern and New Age “meditation” that empties the mind, seeks altered consciousness, or turns inward to the self—the very opposite of filling the mind with the truth of God.

expand to see more

The gravest corruption of meditation is its confusion with the Eastern and mystical practices that bear the same name but are its very opposite. Hindu, Buddhist, and New Age ‘meditation’ seek to empty the mind—to still all thought, to detach from the rational and the verbal, to reach an altered state of consciousness, to merge with an impersonal divine or to turn inward and find the self. Transcendental meditation, mindfulness emptied of God, mantras and breathing techniques aimed at vacancy—these are spiritually perilous, for a mind made empty is not made safe but made vulnerable, and the practices are bound up with pagan and pantheistic religion. This is not biblical meditation but its counterfeit and inversion.

Biblical meditation does not empty the mind but fills it—with the Word, works, and character of God. It is not the suspension of thought but the deepening of it; not detachment from truth but absorption in it; not the inward turn to the self but the outward and upward turn to God. The believer is to take a portion of Scripture or a truth about God and ponder it, mutter it over, chew on it, apply it to his heart, and turn it into prayer—day and night, as the blessed man of the first psalm. This is the bridge between reading and praying, the digestion of spiritual food by which truth descends from the head into the heart and out into the life. The recovery of biblical meditation, which the Puritans prized and the modern church has largely lost, is the recovery of a means of grace by which the soul is nourished, stabilized, and transformed—not by emptying itself into vacancy, but by filling itself with the living God revealed in His Word.

Hebrew Roots

The doctrine rests on hāgāh (to murmur, ponder) and síach (to muse) the law of the LORD day and night—filling the mind with God, not emptying it.
